summary: Defines a template-package for the SIP event framework that reports watcher information, meaning the set of users subscribed to a resource in a given event package. This information changes as people subscribe, unsubscribe or are approved.

eli5.summary: Watcher information lets you see who is looking at your status. This document says how to ask for the list of lookers.

questions: who is subscribed to my presence
what is a sip template package
how does sip presence authorization work
subtitle: How to subscribe to the list of people who are subscribed to your SIP presence, or to any other event.

tldr.problem: When someone subscribes to a user's presence, that user's software has to find out so the subscription can be approved or rejected. There was no standard way to follow the changing set of subscribers.
tldr.mechanism: A template-package named winfo is appended to any event package name (for example presence.winfo), so a user can subscribe to the subscriptions themselves and receive NOTIFY requests that carry watcher information documents.
tldr.outcome: It supports presence authorization and services such as blacklist alerts, with security guidance because the data is sensitive and can be abused for denial of service. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Notification rate limit
facts.value: No faster than once every 5 seconds per subscriber (RECOMMENDED)

today: RFC 3857 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The XML document format it relies on is defined in RFC 3858.

sections.title: Subscribing to Subscriptions
sections.content:
The SIP event framework of RFC 3265 defines the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods and the idea of a package, a concrete use of the framework for a class of events such as user presence. This RFC defines a template-package: a package with all the properties of a regular one, but always tied to another package and applicable to any package, including itself.

For any event package there is a set of subscriptions made by users who want to learn the state of a resource. That set changes as people subscribe, subscriptions expire, and owners approve or reject them. The set of subscribers and the state of their subscriptions is called watcher information. Since it is dynamic, it makes sense to subscribe to it.
sections.eli5: A list of people who are watching you changes all the time. This lets you sign up to hear about changes to that list.

sections.title: The winfo Naming Rule
sections.content:
The template-package is named winfo. The watcher information for any package foo is named foo.winfo, so the people subscribed to presence are described by presence.winfo. Recursion is allowed, so foo.winfo.winfo is a valid name.

Because the document is about subscriptions to subscriptions, it fixes some vocabulary. A watcherinfo subscription is a subscription to watcher information, and a watcherinfo subscriber is the user who made it. Unqualified, subscription means the inner one being monitored, and a watcher is a subscriber to the inner resource.
sections.eli5: Add the word winfo after any event name to mean who is watching it, like presence.winfo for who is watching your presence.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The motivating use is presence authorization. When A subscribes to B's presence, the subscription often needs a human decision. B's client subscribes to presence.winfo for B. When A subscribes, B receives a NOTIFY whose body is an application/watcherinfo+xml document showing a watcher with status="pending", meaning it is awaiting authorization. B's software can alert B, who can then set policy.

A second scenario is blacklist alerts. A user signs up with an application provider, whose server subscribes to the watcher information for that user's presence. When someone subscribes to the user, the application checks the watcher against a database of known bad guys and sends the user email on a match. The user must allow the application to subscribe to the user's presence.winfo.
sections.eli5: When a new person asks to see your status, your phone taps you on the shoulder and says, "Someone new wants to look. Is that okay?"

sections.title: Package Rules: Bodies, Duration and Rate
sections.content:
A SUBSCRIBE for watcher information MAY carry a body that filters the subscription, though its definition is out of scope. Without one, the default policy applies: a notification is sent on every change, a notification triggered by a SUBSCRIBE carries full state (all watchers the subscriber may know about), and one triggered by a change carries only the watcher whose state changed.

There is no good default lifetime for a watcherinfo subscription, so the RFC arbitrarily chooses one hour. Clients SHOULD use an Expires header field to state what they want. Notification bodies use application/watcherinfo+xml, which all subscribers and notifiers MUST support and list in any Accept header. Servers SHOULD NOT send watcherinfo notifications to one subscriber faster than once every 5 seconds.

Watcher information is sensitive, so subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and then authorized. The RECOMMENDED policy is that user A can subscribe to A's own watcher information for any package, and that another user B who is an authorized subscriber to A in package foo can subscribe to foo.winfo for A, but receives only the state of B's own subscription. To avoid endless recursion, only A should be allowed to subscribe to foo.winfo.winfo for A, and deeper levels should not be authorized by default.
sections.eli5: By default you hear about every change, the first answer gives the whole list, and later ones only tell you what is new. The sign-up lasts an hour unless you ask for something else.

sections.title: The Subscription State Machine
sections.content:
To describe a collection of subscriptions, the RFC specifies a model subscription state machine, derived mostly from RFC 3265 with an added waiting state. It is only a model; implementations map their own machinery onto it.

A new subscription starts in the transient init state. If policy forbids it, it goes straight to terminated. If policy authorizes it, it goes to active, and the subscriber receives notifications. With no policy it goes to pending, where no notifications are generated while the server waits for a decision. Approval moves it to active and rejection to terminated. If a pending subscription times out it moves to waiting.

The point of waiting is that a user who was offline can later fetch watcher information and still learn about subscription attempts that arrived earlier. Without it, an expired pending subscription would be destroyed and the user might never hear of it. A new subscription with identical parameters from the same watcher ends the old waiting state with a giveup event. A giveup timer in pending or waiting frees resources; it should be long enough that a user can log in days later and see the attempt. Servers should limit how many pending or waiting subscriptions one subscriber may hold, because that state can feed denial of service attacks.

At any time the server can deactivate a subscription or put it on probation, and a subscription ends with noresource if the resource no longer exists. Notifications MAY be sent on transitions, but they SHOULD NOT be sent for transient states, so a fetch (a SUBSCRIBE with Expires of 0) that passes through init, active and terminated produces none.
sections.eli5: A new request waits in a queue until you say yes or no. If you are away too long it moves to a note on your desk, so you still find out when you return.

sections.title: Forking and State Agents
sections.content:
When many servers share the subscriptions for a resource, no single one has the full list. The RFC allows several solutions without mandating one. In the first, a special proxy forks the watcherinfo SUBSCRIBE to every server that might hold subscriptions, and every one of them accepts it. The subscriber then gets several NOTIFY requests, each opening its own dialog, and combines them. For this to be interoperable, watcherinfo subscribers MUST be prepared to install multiple subscriptions from a single SUBSCRIBE.

In the second, a farm of state agents each knows the entire watcherinfo state for some set of resources. The SUBSCRIBE is routed to the right agent, and the subscriber has only one dialog. How the agents learn the full state is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If the guest list is split between several doorkeepers, you can either ask all of them and combine their answers, or ask one special keeper who has the whole list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two risks are called out. First, denial of service: a resource with many watchers can produce a large stream of notifications. Watcherinfo subscriptions should be allowed only from explicitly authorized, authenticated entities. Even then, an attacker could create many ordinary subscriptions to flood a user who watches their own watcher information, with amplification of two if a notification is sent on creation and another on termination, and the data volume could be the square of what the attacker sends if each notification carries full state. Servers should never create subscription state, or send watcherinfo notifications, for unauthenticated SUBSCRIBE requests.

Second, divulging sensitive information: for presence, watcher information reveals a person's friends, family and business relations. To defend against eavesdropping, watchers MAY use the sips scheme, notifiers MUST support TLS and sips as if they were proxies, and S/MIME MAY be used end to end. Against spoofed subscriptions, all watcherinfo subscriptions should be authenticated and authorized, and the RFC notes that all watchers MUST support HTTP Digest.
sections.eli5: A list of who is watching you tells a lot about your friends. So only the right people should see it, and a bully should not be able to make your phone buzz endlessly.
